questions.title: What is the purpose of the stabilizer state $m_t$ in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the section on sLSTM and I see that they introduce exponential activation functions for the input and forget gates. The paper mentions that these can lead to overflows and introduces a stabilizer state $m_t$ defined as $m_t = \max ( \log ( f_t ) + m_{t-1} , \log ( i_t ) )$. I don't quite understand how subtracting $m_t$ from the log-gates in the stabilized versions $i'_t$ and $f'_t$ prevents overflow without changing the actual output of the network.

questions.title: How does exponential gating allow the model to 'revise' storage decisions?
questions.question_body: In the introduction, the authors claim that standard LSTMs are unable to revise storage decisions, specifically citing the Nearest Neighbor Search problem. They argue that xLSTM remediates this through exponential gating. Conceptually, why does changing the gate activation from a sigmoid $\sigma(x)$ to an exponential $\exp(x)$ enable the model to 'overwrite' or 'revise' a previously stored value in the cell state $c_t$ more effectively?

questions.title: Why is mLSTM parallelizable while sLSTM is not?
questions.question_body: The paper states that mLSTM is fully parallelizable, whereas sLSTM is not due to 'memory mixing' (hidden-hidden connections). From what I understand, both are recurrent models. Specifically, what is the 'memory mixing' in sLSTM that creates this sequential dependency, and why does the matrix memory structure of mLSTM remove the need for this specific type of recurrence, allowing it to be computed in parallel?

questions.title: Relationship between mLSTM matrix memory and Transformer attention
questions.question_body: The mLSTM uses a covariance update rule $\mathbf{C}_t = f_t \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$ and retrieves information via $\mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t$. This looks very similar to the key-value retrieval mechanism in Transformers. Is the matrix $\mathbf{C}_t$ essentially acting as a compressed representation of the KV cache? If so, how does the use of a fixed-size $d \times d$ matrix differ from the growing KV cache in a standard Transformer in terms of what information is preserved?

questions.title: Clarification on Pre vs. Post Up-Projection in xLSTM blocks
questions.question_body: The paper mentions two types of residual block architectures based on Cover's Theorem: post up-projection (used for sLSTM) and pre up-projection (used for mLSTM). The authors state that for mLSTM, pre up-projection is used because 'the memory capacity becomes larger in the high-dimensional space.' I'm confused about the logic here: if we project to a higher dimension *before* the mLSTM layer, does that mean the matrix memory $\mathbf{C}_t$ itself is larger, or just that the vectors $\mathbf{k}_t$ and $\mathbf{v}_t$ are larger?
